coverage_limitations: 168 of 1758 abusers on the validation worlds have fewer than three mature sale lines and are outside the ranking.
165 of 1773 abusers on the final test worlds are outside the ranking for the same reason.
Simulated data from one generator: results show stability across simulated worlds, not performance on real returns.

Two signals carry the model: how much of what a customer asks back is a transaction claim, and item returns made late in the return window. Out of fold on training worlds its precision is 77% with all features, 64% without the claim features, 61% without the timing features and 38% without both, against 23% for the return-rate rule. How sharply both signals separate abusers is a setting of this simulation.

Honest customers with two or more genuinely failed deliveries are sent for review more often by the model than by the return-rate rule (10.7% against 5.9% on training worlds, out of fold) and are 63% of the model's false positives. The gate has a leg for this group; this figure is from training worlds.

Honest customers with exactly one genuinely failed delivery have a gate leg of their own, so that protecting repeat claimants is not paid for by reviewing them instead: the model sends 1.6% of them for review against 5.0% for the return-rate rule (training worlds, out of fold).

The level of the result follows the simulated behaviour: across the 11 stress worlds the selected model's precision ranges from 35% to 88% and the rule's from 13% to 40%; the model passes the gate on 2 of them. Quote the gap to the rule, not the level.
The heavy-returner group is defined on return rate itself, so that gate leg cannot fail for a model and is not evidence.
